## About Me

I am a PhD candidate in Economics at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, expected to graduate in May 2027. I am on the **2026–27 academic job market**.

My research lies at the intersection of **environmental, urban, and spatial economics**. I study how environmental risks and natural disasters affect housing markets, households, and local economic outcomes.

My research uses spatial, administrative, environmental, economic, weather, and nighttime-lights data to examine the economic effects of environmental risks and shocks.

I also have experience in applied economic policy research through my work as a Short-Term Consultant with the **World Bank Group** in the Nepal Country Office.

## Research Interests

**Primary**: Economic Development, Real Estate Economics, Environmental Economics

**Secondary**: International Economics

## Job Market Paper

[**Water Contamination and Real Estate Prices: Evidence from Hawaii's Red Hill Fuel Leak**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1brv0YUjsXEcLBAMBpzzSRgo_wUgt2wDG/view?usp=sharing)

This paper examines the effects of the 2021 Red Hill fuel leak on residential property values on Oahu, Hawaii. Exploiting the leak as a quasi-experimental shock within a difference-in-differences framework, I compare changes in single-family home prices in potentially exposed areas with those in unexposed control areas before and after the event. The results indicate that properties within the potentially exposed area experienced an average price decline of approximately 16.8 percent following the leak, with the estimated discount largest in the second year after the event. These findings are robust to alternative spatial treatment definitions, a placebo test centered on the 2014 fuel release, and a specification that explicitly accounts for spatial spillovers. Finally, analysis of transaction probabilities yields a negative but statistically insignificant effect, suggesting that housing-market adjustment is more evident in property prices than in the likelihood of a sale.
